feat.title: Feature Design
feat.subtitle: Three capability domains, nine core features
feat.c1.desc: 64-bit, k-ordered, globally unique; roughly 500k IDs per second per process with no central coordinator and no database round-trip.
feat.c2.desc: Timestamp, datacenter, worker and sequence widths are all configurable; the default 5+5+12 layout supports 1024 nodes.
feat.c3.desc: Decompose any generated ID back into its timestamp, datacenter, worker and sequence parts — useful for debugging and sharding.
feat.c4.desc: The sequence resolver is an interface; two implementations ship built in, and a Redis-backed shared sequence is a few lines away.
feat.c5.desc: A configurable tolerance window absorbs NTP jitter; anything beyond it throws instead of risking duplicate IDs.
feat.c6.desc: Laravel, Webman, ThinkPHP and Hyperf work out of the box, with auto-discovery and container integration.
feat.c7.desc: Config arrays, config files and environment variables all land in one validated factory that rejects impossible combinations.
feat.c8.desc: Five exception types, each carrying the offending value and its limit, so the message points straight at the misconfiguration.
feat.c9.desc: A full PHPUnit suite, a PHP 8.0–8.4 CI matrix, and automatic versioning on every push to main.
feat.footer: Runtime: PHP >= 8.0 (CI covers 8.0 – 8.4) · 64-bit system · one instance per process or coroutine, sequence state is never shared
life.title: ID Lifecycle
life.subtitle: One id() call: the full path, the state it touches, and the limits it respects
life.bits.title: ID layout (64 bits by default)
life.bits.l1: Sign bit 1 (always 0); timestamp = milliseconds since the epoch
life.bits.l3: Sequence 12 bits = 4096 IDs per millisecond (default layout)
life.state.title: Instance state (kept across calls)
life.state.l1: lastTimestamp — the millisecond of the previous ID, used for drift and exhaustion checks
life.state.l2: sequenceResolver — the sequence cursor for the current millisecond (seq / lastTs)
life.state.l3: fixedBits / epoch — node bits and start time, read-only after construction
life.state.note: Note: an instance must never be shared across processes or coroutines
life.cap.title: Capacity & throughput
life.cap.l1: At most 2^12 = 4096 IDs per millisecond; beyond that it spins to the next millisecond.
life.cap.l2: Roughly 500k IDs per second in a single process.
life.cap.l3: Nodes claim a unique (datacenter_id, worker_id) pair; the default layout allows 32 × 32 = 1024 nodes.
life.time.title: Lifetime timeline
life.time.l4: A more recent epoch resets the full lifespan.
life.flow.n1.cap: Read the current millisecond; it is the time base for this ID.
life.flow.d1.cap: Yes → if the drift is within clock_tolerance_ms, reuse the previous millisecond; otherwise throw ClockDriftException and refuse to generate.
life.flow.n2.cap: offset is the distance in milliseconds from the configured epoch.
life.flow.d2.cap: Yes → a clock before the epoch throws ClockDriftException; an exhausted epoch throws TimestampOverflowException.
life.flow.n3.cap: When the sequence is exhausted (null) it spins to the next millisecond and retries once, then fails with a RuntimeException.
life.flow.n4.cap: State only advances once every guard has passed, so a failed call cannot poison the next one.
